Issue #14 — T. S. Eliot: The Waste Land: III. The Fire Sermon

AJL14154 Modern Anglophone Poetry | 2026年10月23日 | Week: T. S. Eliot (1) — Prufrock / The Waste Land

I. Poet Biography — Eliot, Spenser and the Thames

Section III takes its title from the Buddha's "Fire Sermon" (the Ādittapariyāya Sutta), in which all the senses are said to be burning with the fire of passion. Eliot's notes compare its importance to that of the Sermon on the Mount, and the section ends by setting the Buddha's sermon beside Saint Augustine's Confessions ("To Carthage then I came") (Rainey, 2006).

The refrain "Sweet Thames, run softly, till I end my song" comes from Edmund Spenser's "Prothalamion" (1596), a celebratory poem written for a double aristocratic wedding on the Thames. Eliot sets Spenser's festive river against the litter and abandoned pleasures of the modern Thames (Ricks & McCue, 2015).

Eliot wrote part of this section at Margate in the autumn of 1921 ("On Margate Sands" appears later in the same section). He had studied Sanskrit and Pali texts at Harvard between 1911 and 1914, which informs the Buddhist frame of the section (Crawford, 2015).

Sources: Crawford, R. (2015). Young Eliot: From St Louis to The Waste Land. Jonathan Cape. | Gordon, L. (1998). T. S. Eliot: An Imperfect Life. Norton. | Ricks, C., & McCue, J. (Eds.). (2015). The Poems of T. S. Eliot (2 vols.). Faber & Faber. | Rainey, L. (Ed.). (2006). The Annotated Waste Land. Yale UP.

II. The Poem — The Waste Land, III. The Fire Sermon, lines 173-186

From The Waste Land (1922)

The river's tent is broken: the last fingers of leaf
Clutch and sink into the wet bank. The wind
Crosses the brown land, unheard. The nymphs are departed.
Sweet Thames, run softly, till I end my song.
The river bears no empty bottles, sandwich papers,
Silk handkerchiefs, cardboard boxes, cigarette ends
Or other testimony of summer nights. The nymphs are departed.
And their friends, the loitering heirs of city directors;
Departed, have left no addresses.
By the waters of Leman I sat down and wept . . .
Sweet Thames, run softly till I end my song,
Sweet Thames, run softly, for I speak not loud or long.
But at my back in a cold blast I hear
The rattle of the bones, and chuckle spread from ear to ear.

“By the waters of Leman I sat down and wept”改写自《诗篇》第 137 篇“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept”。Leman 是日内瓦湖（莱芒湖）的旧称，也是一个古英语词，意为“情人”。Eliot 就是在洛桑（湖边）写完这首诗的。“But at my back...”则仿 Marvell《To His Coy Mistress》中的“But at my back I always hear / Time's wingèd chariot hurrying near”。

Vocabulary Notes

Word Phonetic Definition Example
clutch /klʌtʃ/ 紧抓，攥住 The child clutched her mother's hand.
nymph /nɪmf/ （神话中的）仙女，宁芙 In the myth, a nymph lived in every spring.
testimony /ˈtestɪməni/ 证词；证据 The ruins are testimony to the city's past wealth.
loiter /ˈlɔɪtə(r)/ 闲荡，游荡 Teenagers loitered outside the shop.
heir /eə(r)/ 继承人 He was the sole heir to the family fortune.
rattle /ˈrætl/ 嘎嘎声，咔哒声 We heard the rattle of the windows in the storm.
chuckle /ˈtʃʌkl/ 咯咯笑，暗笑 He chuckled at his own joke.

III. Close Reading Prompts

The following questions adopt a New Critical approach, focusing on textual evidence — imagery, structure, diction, ambiguity, paradox, and irony — rather than biographical or historical context.

1. Negative catalogue. "The river bears no empty bottles, sandwich papers, / Silk handkerchiefs..." The rubbish is listed only to say it is absent. What is the effect of this negative description? Does the river feel cleaner or more desolate?

2. Spenser's refrain. How does the line "Sweet Thames, run softly, till I end my song" sound when it is placed among bottles and cigarette ends? Is Eliot mocking the modern city, Spenser's idealism, or neither?

3. "The nymphs are departed." The phrase is repeated. Who are the nymphs: mythical figures, or the young women of "summer nights"? How does the double meaning work with "loitering heirs of city directors"?

4. Exile and lament. "By the waters of Leman I sat down and wept" rewrites Psalm 137, the song of the Jews in Babylonian exile. What kind of exile is the speaker in? Consider the double meaning of "Leman".

5. The turn to death. The last two lines replace Marvell's "Time's wingèd chariot" with "The rattle of the bones". How does this rewriting change the tone from urgency to horror or grotesque comedy?

IV. Research Frontiers

1. Kearns, Cleo McNelly. T. S. Eliot and Indic Traditions: A Study in Poetry and Belief. Cambridge UP, 1987.
[Monograph, library access]
Relevance: The standard English-language study of Eliot's engagement with Hindu and Buddhist texts, from his Harvard studies to The Waste Land and Four Quartets. Directly relevant to the Buddhist title of this section.

2. 张剑. 《艾略特与印度：〈荒原〉和〈四个四重奏〉中的佛教、印度教思想》.
[已在你的 Notion 文献库中]
Relevance: 可以和 Kearns 的英文研究对照着读，看中国学者怎样解读同一组宗教材料。你的 Notion 里还有洪增流《〈荒原〉的宗教思想主线的重新探讨》，同样可以作为这一节的参考。

3. Rainey, Lawrence, ed. The Annotated Waste Land with Eliot's Contemporary Prose. 2nd ed. Yale UP, 2006.
[Annotated edition, library access]
Relevance: Annotates the Spenser, Psalm, Marvell and Buddhist allusions in this passage, and reprints Eliot's notes on the Fire Sermon and Augustine.

issues.html_body:
Issue #15 — T. S. Eliot: The Waste Land: V. What the Thunder Said

AJL14154 Modern Anglophone Poetry | 2026年10月24日 | Week: T. S. Eliot (1) — Prufrock / The Waste Land

I. Poet Biography — The Thunder and the Upanishad

The closing section draws on a fable in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (5.2). The creator Prajāpati answers gods, humans and demons with the single syllable "DA", which each group interprets differently: datta (give), dayadhvam (be compassionate) and damyata (control yourselves). Eliot's notes refer readers to Paul Deussen's German translation, Sechzig Upanishads des Veda (Rainey, 2006).

In his notes Eliot also explained that the first part of section V uses three themes: the journey to Emmaus, the approach to the Chapel Perilous of the Grail legend, and "the present decay of eastern Europe". The section moves from a parched, rocky landscape to the coming of rain over the Ganges ("Ganga") and the Himalaya ("Himavant") (Rainey, 2006).

The poem ends with a sequence of quotations in several languages and with "Shantih shantih shantih", the formal ending of an Upanishad. Eliot's note glosses it as "The Peace which passeth understanding", a phrase from Saint Paul's Letter to the Philippians (Ricks & McCue, 2015).

Sources: Crawford, R. (2015). Young Eliot: From St Louis to The Waste Land. Jonathan Cape. | Gordon, L. (1998). T. S. Eliot: An Imperfect Life. Norton. | Ricks, C., & McCue, J. (Eds.). (2015). The Poems of T. S. Eliot (2 vols.). Faber & Faber. | Rainey, L. (Ed.). (2006). The Annotated Waste Land. Yale UP.

II. The Poem — The Waste Land, V. What the Thunder Said, lines 424-433

From The Waste Land (1922)

                                        I sat upon the shore
Fishing, with the arid plain behind me
Shall I at least set my lands in order?
London Bridge is falling down falling down falling down
Poi s'ascose nel foco che gli affina
Quando fiam uti chelidon—O swallow swallow
Le Prince d'Aquitaine à la tour abolie
These fragments I have shored against my ruins
Why then Ile fit you. Hieronymo's mad againe.
Datta. Dayadhvam. Damyata.
                    Shantih shantih shantih

这是全诗最后 10 行，几乎每行都引自别的作品：意大利语出自但丁《炼狱篇》第 26 歌（“然后他隐入那炼净他们的火中”）；拉丁语出自《维纳斯节前夜》（“我何时才能像燕子一样？”）；法语出自 Nerval 的十四行诗《El Desdichado》（“阿基坦王子在废弃的塔中”）；倒数第三行出自 Kyd 的《西班牙悲剧》。

Vocabulary Notes

Word Phonetic Definition Example
arid /ˈærɪd/ 干旱的，贫瘠的 Few crops grow in this arid region.
shore /ʃɔː(r)/ （动词）用支柱撑住（shore up）；（名词）海岸 They shored up the wall with wooden beams.
fragment /ˈfræɡmənt/ 碎片，片段 Only fragments of the poem survive.
abolish /əˈbɒlɪʃ/ 废除；（此处法语 abolie）被毁的 Slavery was abolished in the British Empire in 1833.
datta /ˈdʌtə/ （梵语）给予 In the fable, datta is the first meaning heard in the thunder.
shantih /ˈʃɑːnti/ （梵语 śānti）平静，安宁 The Upanishads end with the threefold shantih.

III. Close Reading Prompts

The following questions adopt a New Critical approach, focusing on textual evidence — imagery, structure, diction, ambiguity, paradox, and irony — rather than biographical or historical context.

1. The Fisher King. "I sat upon the shore / Fishing, with the arid plain behind me" recalls the Fisher King of the Grail legends, whose wound made his land barren. Why does the speaker face the sea and turn his back on the plain? What does "set my lands in order" ask for?

2. "These fragments." "These fragments I have shored against my ruins". Read the line as the poem's own description of itself. Does it present fragmentation as failure or as a strategy for survival? Consider the pun in "shored" (to prop up / the shore).

3. Languages in sequence. The lines move through English, Italian, Latin, French and Sanskrit. Does the reader need to translate them to feel their effect? What is gained or lost if you read them as sound only?

4. "Hieronymo's mad againe." In Kyd's play, Hieronymo pretends to be mad in order to take revenge. Why does Eliot quote this line just before the Sanskrit words? What does it suggest about the poet's own role in assembling the fragments?

5. Ending on peace? The poem ends with "Shantih" repeated three times. Is this a genuine resolution, a hope, or an ironic gesture in a poem about ruin? Consider whether a Western reader can share the peace of a formula in another tradition.

IV. Research Frontiers

1. Kearns, Cleo McNelly. T. S. Eliot and Indic Traditions: A Study in Poetry and Belief. Cambridge UP, 1987.
[Monograph, library access]
Relevance: Discusses the thunder fable of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad and the meaning of "Shantih" in Eliot's ending, arguing that Indic thought is more than decoration in the poem.

2. Eliot, Valerie, ed. The Waste Land: A Facsimile and Transcript of the Original Drafts Including the Annotations of Ezra Pound. Faber & Faber, 1971.
[Primary source, library access]
Relevance: Shows that "What the Thunder Said" was the section Pound changed least, which makes it a useful case for comparing Eliot's own composition with the parts Pound reshaped.

3. 文玲霞；王光林. 《艾略特〈荒原〉里的音景》；《人类世时代再读〈荒原〉》.
[已在你的 Notion 文献库中]
Relevance: 两篇都可以接着今天的结尾来读：一篇从声音和音景入手（雷声、鸟鸣、多语种的引文），一篇从生态与人类世的角度重读“荒原”的意象。
